flawed_step: Step 3: the claim that P(|X_n − X| > eps) is bounded by an expression in the marginal CDFs F_{X_n} and F_X alone. That probability depends on the joint law of (X_n, X), and the marginals do not determine it.
counterexample: Let X take the values +1 and −1 with probability 1/2 each, and set X_n = −X for every n. Then F_{X_n} = F_X, so X_n → X in distribution. But |X_n − X| = 2 always, so P(|X_n − X| > 1) = 1 for every n. So X_n does not converge to X in probability.
assessment_summary:
Proof attempt:
1. Fix eps > 0. The goal is P(|X_n − X| > eps) → 0. — Justified: this is the definition of convergence in probability.
2. By hypothesis, F_{X_n}(t) → F_X(t) at every continuity point t of F_X. — Justified: this is the hypothesis as defined.
3. Bound P(|X_n − X| > eps) by an expression in F_{X_n} and F_X only, for example using the events {X_n ≤ t} and {X > t + eps}. — NOT justified. The event {|X_n − X| > eps} depends on the joint distribution of (X_n, X). Convergence in distribution only controls each marginal separately and says nothing about how X_n and X are coupled. No bound of this kind can hold in general.
4. Let n → ∞ in that bound and use step 2 to get a limit of 0. — Not justified, because it rests on step 3. It would also need care at discontinuity points of F_X.
5. Conclude X_n → X in probability. — Not justified, because it depends on steps 3–4.

The gap cannot be fixed, because the statement is false. Take X = ±1 with probability 1/2 each and X_n = −X. Then X_n has the same distribution as X, so convergence in distribution holds trivially. However, |X_n − X| = 2, so P(|X_n − X| > 1) = 1 for all n. The statement is a known false converse. It becomes true when X is almost surely a constant, but that restriction is not part of the claim.
